To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) human repetitive elements, including transposable elements and other repetitive sequences, have the potential to influence the expression of nearby genes, and 2) this potential is revealed in the mouse genome by changes in DNA methlyation and chromatin structure that occur in the mouse germline.
human-specific repetitive elements can be transcriptionally activated when placed into a heterologous environment in a transchromosomically transmitted chromosome.
a heterologus regulatory environment can activate transposon derived regulatory regions in a mouse genome and that these regions correspond to changes in DNA Methylation at CpG Dinucleotides.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the regulation of the repetitive genome.
the evolutionary and functional significance of repetitive elements in the human genome.
understanding the mechanisms that control the expression of transposable elements (TEs).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the repetitive human genome is not as silent as previously thought.
the repetitive human genome has the latent regulatory potential, which is species specific.
human transposon elements are capable of activating gene expression in a mouse background.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the human-specific repetitive genome has latent regulatory potential.

human-specific repetitive elements can be activated in the mouse nucleus, and that this is accompanied by a change in DNA methylation and histone modifications at CpG dinucelotides, suggesting a mechanism for their silencing in human cells.

human repetitive elements are transcriptionally repressed in the human germline and somatic cell genome, but that this repression is relaxed in the mouse germline and to a lesser degree in somatic cells, leading to activation of these repetitive elements in the mouse genome.
The main takeaway from our work is that
transposable elements are not just junk, and that they have the potential to be activated and regulate gene expression in the human genome.
the regulatory environment can influence the transcriptional activity of repetitive sequences, even when they are located far from their cognate genes.
the repetitive human genome contains latent regulatory elements that can be activated by changes in epigenetic state.
